Q: + symbol in 7th column in COBOL A:

Plus is not standard anymore. not 100% certain, but I believe it's for double spacing the output, similar to / for page eject. Ignore it.

Q: ASP.NET Core OpenAPI/SwaggerUI XML root collections "XML example cannot be generated; root element name is undefined" A:

Your problem is that you are trying to use the data contract serializer to serialize your models to XML -- but neither WeatherForecasts nor WeatherForecast can actually be serialized by this serializer.

Your specific problems are:

  1. DataContractSerializer does not support collections that lack a parameterless constructor.

    If I try to serialize your WeatherForecasts collection, I get an error

    System.Runtime.Serialization.InvalidDataContractException: Type 'WeatherForecasts' with CollectionDataContractAttribute attribute is an invalid collection type since it does not have a default constructor.

    See demo #1 here.

    The error seems clear -- DataContractSerializer only supports collections with parameterless constructors. This serializer dates from .NET 3.5 and it seems it just doesn't support such newfangled things as primary constructors; you need to either remove the primary constructor or add a parameterless constructor.

  2. DataContractSerializer does not support serializing of get-only properties.

    Your WeatherForecast model has a property

    [DataMember]
public int TemperatureF => 32 + (int)(TemperatureC / 0.5556);

    If I try to serialize this model standalone, I get an error

    System.Runtime.Serialization.InvalidDataContractException: No set method for property 'TemperatureF' in type 'WeatherForecast'.

    Demo #2 here.

    I can't find any place in the documentation where this restriction is stated other than when running in "partial trust", [1] but again the error seems clear.

    To fix the error, you can add a dummy private setter (unless you are running in partial trust in which case the setter must be public. However partial trust isn't even supported in .NET Core / .NET 5+ so this shouldn't matter for you. [2])

Putting all this together, if you fix your data models as follows you should be able to serialize and deserialize them using XmlDataContractSerializerOutputFormatter and XmlDataContractSerializerInputFormatter:

[CollectionDataContract(Name = "forecasts")]
public sealed class WeatherForecasts(IList<WeatherForecast> list) : Collection<WeatherForecast>(list)
{
    // FIX: add parameterless constructor required by DataContractSerializer
    public WeatherForecasts() : this(new List<WeatherForecast>()){}
}


[DataContract(Name = "forecast")]
public class WeatherForecast 
{
    [DataMember]
    public DateOnly Date { get; set; }

    [DataMember]
    public int TemperatureC { get; set; }

    [DataMember] 
    // FIX: add dummy private setter required by DataContractSerializer
    public int TemperatureF { get => 32 + (int)(TemperatureC / 0.5556); private set { } }

    [DataMember]
    public string? Summary { get; set; }
}

Demo #3 here.

[1] "Partial trust" was a feature of .NET Framework that allowed certain code to be executed in a "less trusted" mode where certain APIs would be unavailable. See Partial trust for details.

[2] See Differences with WPF .NET: Code Access Security.

Q: Architecture for handling OAuth token refresh across multiple services in agent-based systems A:

A few behaviors to consider.

TOKEN REFRESH

Only user-facing clients (e.g. a browser app or mobile app) should initiate token refresh requests. Multiple views or frontend workers must synchronise token refresh, e.g.:

  • Queue up a collection of promises.
  • Only the first promise runs a refresh.
  • All promises return the same refresh result.

The result should be short-lived tokens (or cookies that represent tokens), e.g. with a 15 minute lifetime. The short lifetime helps to mitigate token (or cookie) interception threats.

BACKEND WORKLOADS

These should not need to synchronise and each replica should receive user-level access tokens when a user is present. That keeps user attributes cryptographically verifiable and auditable.

When no user is present, e.g. for a nightly job, backend replicas can each get their own access token with the same client credential, without conflicts.

TOKEN EXCHANGE

A common option is to receive an access token from an internet client. For example, a web portal could use the A2A protocol to send a natural language command to a backend agent.

However, the web portal may have more scopes than you want the agent to receive. Therefore, an API gateway can use OAuth Token Exchange to downscope the access token before routing to the agent. Doing so maintains user identity attributes within the exchanged token.

Token exchange is often accompanied by in-memory caching. For example, with the hash of the original user-level access token as the cache key and the exchanged token as the cache value.

FEDERATION

Ideally. token exchange should span organizations, each of which could implement the Identity Assertion Grant, a federated form of token exchange.

When that is not possible, you may need to get a third-party token in other ways, e.g with the client credentials grant. You may be able to continue to use an incoming access token as a cache key, so that you keep third-party tokens in the backend.

SUMMARY

In OAuth, an up to date authorization server should issue tokens that enable the following behaviours, none of which should require complex code:

  • Frontend components use token refresh to balance good usability with short-lived HTTP credentials.

  • Resource servers use access tokens from their trusted issuer, and you can dictate scopes and claims that each client and resource server receives in access tokens.

  • Token exchange enables you to control tokens, to change their scopes and claims, as tokens flow between backend components.

If agents ever behave unpredictably, and try to perform operations outside of their remit, token attributes should enable resource servers to deny access.

Q: Version of Activeweb for Tomcat v.10 A:

Upgrade to Tomcat 10.1 (recommended). Since JavaLite 3.5.j11 targets Jakarta Servlet 6.1, the minimum required container is Tomcat 10.1

AI-generated content is not allowed.

Q: Aggregate multiple columns by the sum of next column A:

This can be done with findgroups (or unique) and accumarray as follows:

game_labels = findgroups(game); % or: [~, ~, game_labels] = unique(game)
money_labels = findgroups(Money); % or [~, ~, money_labels] = unique(Money)
y = accumarray([game_labels money_labels], Score, ...
    [max(game_labels) max(money_labels)], @sum, 0);

Take a look at the documentation of the used functions (links above), which should make the code easy to follow.

Q: RMarkdown table captions for multiple tables are rendered incorrectly when knitting to a Microsoft Word document A:

That's Microsoft Word's fault. It decides that two tables with no break between them is the same table.

---
title: "Untitled"
author: "Anyone"
date: "2/29/2020"
output:
  word_document: default
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(dplyr)
library(flextable)

knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE,message=FALSE)

```


```{r Table1}
cars1<-cars*0+1
theme_zebra(flextable(cars1))%>% 
  align(align="center",part="all") %>% 
  autofit%>% 
  add_header_lines(paste("Table 1: Model output for thing 1"))

```

blah

```{r Table2}
cars2<-cars*0+2
theme_zebra(flextable(cars2))%>% 
  align(align="center",part="all") %>% 
  autofit%>% 
  add_header_lines(paste("Table 2: Model output for thing 2"))

```

blah

```{r Table3}
cars3<-cars*0+3
theme_zebra(flextable(cars3))%>% 
  align(align="center",part="all") %>% 
  autofit%>% 
  add_header_lines(paste("Table 3: Model output for thing 3"))

```

blah

```{r Table4}
cars4<-cars*0+4
theme_zebra(flextable(cars4))%>% 
  align(align="center",part="all") %>% 
  autofit%>% 
  add_header_lines(paste("Table 4: Model output for thing 4"))

```

As far as I know, this is not something that can be solved with flextable but if there is an option I am not aware of, I'd be happy to integrate it.
